HSBC Sells $300M Of Data Center Debt Tied To Stargate Project At Big Discount
November 17, 2026 | 3:35 pm ET
Dan Rabb, Data Centers
Financial giant HSBC has sold $300M in data center construction debt at less than 90 cents on the dollar, the latest sign of lender wariness of the growing risks facing large-scale data center development.
Wikimedia Commons/Barry Caruth
The debt is part of an $18B financing package assembled by 20 banks for Project Jupiter, a massive data center development in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, Bloomberg reports . The construction financing closed last year after being marketed to lenders under the code name Project Miner amid a boom in debt financing for hyperscalers ’ artificial intelligence campuses. But Project Jupiter has since run into problems. The 1,400-acre campus is being developed by Blue Owl-backed Stack Infrastructure for OpenAI , Oracle and SoftBank 's Stargate initiative and could eventually reach 2.45 gigawatts. The project has faced concerns about potential delays due to community opposition and regulatory hurdles involving air and pipeline permits. In September, Oracle sent the developers a force majeure notice that would allow it to defer payments if the project is delayed or derailed. HSBC reportedly unloaded the $300M chunk of its debt tied to the project immediately after the force majeure notice, according to Bloomberg. HSBC isn't the only lender that has tried to reduce its exposure to Project Jupiter. Dutch bank ING is also reportedly seeking buyers for $25M of debt backing the development, along with nearly a dozen other data center loans. The debt sales are just the latest sign of growing volatility across data center credit markets. Lenders are showing concerns about escalating risks surrounding data center development — from community opposition and restrictive regulations to uncertainty about the future of AI cloud providers and alarm at the pace of hyperscale infrastructure spending. Jensen Huang ’s sudden resignation from Nvidia has only added to the unease surrounding the sector. Lender anxiety has been most apparent in the structured debt markets. In recent weeks, yields on some bonds tied to data center projects have climbed into the double digits, while even debt issued by major hyperscalers has traded at higher spreads than the investment-grade standard. At the same time, credit default swaps on data center debt have hit an all-time high. Analysts also say the lenders are concerned about concentration risk . The scale of capital required for the AI data center boom is unprecedented, and there is only so much capital that any lender is comfortable having tied up in just a handful of companies all pursuing broadly similar strategies.

HSBC sold US$300mil troubled data centre loan at discount
TheStar
Tue, Nov 17, 2026 03:33pm - 17 hours
View Original
FILE PHOTO: A logo of HSBC is seen on its headquarters at the financial Central district in Hong Kong, China August 4, 2020. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu/File Photo HSBC Holdings Plc offloaded a roughly US$300mil piece of a loan to build a troubled New Mexico data center project at a steep discount, underscoring deepening anxiety surrounding the AI boom. The bank sold the slice of an US$18bil financing package - which funds construction of the campus in Doña Ana County tied to Oracle Corp. - at prices in the mid-80s, according to people familiar with the matter. The sale took place several weeks ago, shortly after Oracle sent a notice to the project’s developer citing force majeure, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. HSBC’s move comes as lenders weigh their exposure to AI debt alongside renewed regulatory pushback following a Democratic sweep. Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia Corp., a linchpin of AI’s rapid expansion, has also triggered concerns about the pace of AI growth. The massive venture in southern New Mexico known as Project Jupiter has been beset by regulatory hurdles and opposition. Oracle sent the force majeure notice to the developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital Inc., in an attempt to put off payments should the venture get derailed, Bloomberg reported in late September.
...
Summary Overview
• HSBC sold a US$300 million portion of an US$18 billion financing package for the troubled Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico at a steep discount, with prices in the mid-80s, signaling deepening anxiety over the sustainability of the AI infrastructure boom.
• The sale occurred shortly after Oracle Corp. issued a force majeure notice to the developer, a Blue Owl Capital unit, to delay payments amid significant regulatory hurdles, including delays in acquiring essential air and pipeline permits for the 2.45-gigawatt campus.
• This move by HSBC reflects a broader trend where lenders are reassessing their exposure to AI-related debt, driven by renewed regulatory scrutiny following a Democratic sweep and market concerns triggered by Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from Nvidia Corp.
• The transaction is notable because banks holding construction project financing loans typically retain them on their balance sheets until completion, meaning early exits often require selling at a discount that exceeds the upfront fees received, as seen in this syndicated loan involving approximately 20 banks.

Blackstone REIT to buy majority stake in US$5b Amazon data centre portfolio Wednesday 18 Nov 2026 BURSA SGX Home Tech Make The Edge Malaysia your preferred source on Google (Nov 16): Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust said on Monday it had agreed to buy a 75.1% controlling stake in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services, in a deal valuing the data centre portfolio at about US$5 billion (RM20.5 billion).
The deal marks the first investment by the recently listed real estate investment trust, which focuses on owning newly constructed data centers leased to large cloud computing companies on long-term contracts.
The two joint ventures will own 13 newly constructed powered shells across two AWS data centre campuses, with Amazon affiliates retaining a 24.9% stake.
AWS will lease back the entire portfolio on a triple net basis with an initial lease term of 12 years and a fully extended lease term of 32 years, the company said.
Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust said it expects to use US$1.9 billion of cash raised through its initial public offering to fund the acquisition
The remaining funding, including transaction costs, is expected to come from about US$2.5 billion in non-recourse mortgage loans secured by the properties.
The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Morgan Stanley, CBRE Capital Markets, Citi, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo Bank are serving as financial advisers on the transaction
